chunks: I asked him about a man who slaughtered a sheep, and it convulsed and fell into a water well while its jugular veins were gushing blood. Can one perform wudu from that well? He said: Draw out from it between thirty and forty buckets, then one may perform wudu from it, and there is no problem with it.

He said: And I asked him about a man who slaughtered a chicken or a dove and it fell into a well. Is it proper to perform wudu from it? He said: Draw out from it a few buckets, then one may perform wudu from it.
And I asked him about a man who is drawing water from a well and his nose bleeds into it. Can one perform wudu from it? He said: Draw out from it a few buckets.

key_terms.أَوْدَاج: jugular veins; the major blood vessels of the neck that are cut in ritual slaughter
key_terms.تَشْخُبُ: to gush or flow forcefully, describing blood spurting from veins
key_terms.دَلْو: a bucket used to draw water from a well
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no harm/objection; a common legal formula indicating permissibility
key_terms.يُنْزَحُ: to draw/exhaust water from a well as a purification measure

ai.seo_question: How many buckets must be drawn from a well that a slaughtered animal fell into to make it pure for wudu according to Imam al-Kazim?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) provides specific jurisprudential rulings on purifying a well contaminated by blood from slaughtered animals or a nosebleed. The ruling distinguishes between the severity of contamination: a large animal bleeding heavily requires thirty to forty buckets to be drawn, while smaller animals or nosebleed requires only a few buckets, after which the well is restored to a state suitable for wudu. This reflects early Islamic jurisprudence's practical approach to ritual purity (tahara), establishing that wells can be purified through exhausting a sufficient quantity of water.
